q: The order and degree of the differential equation (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0 are:
x: The highest derivative is d²y/dx², so the order is 2; its power is 3, so the degree is 3. Taking the power 4 of dy/dx as the degree is the common slip.

q: The order and degree of the differential equation d²y/dx² = √(1 + (dy/dx)²) are:
x: First clear the radical: (d²y/dx²)² = 1 + (dy/dx)². The highest derivative is second order and it now appears squared, so order 2, degree 2. Reading the degree before removing the square root gives degree 1.

q: What is the order of the differential equation d³y/dx³ + 2(d²y/dx²)⁵ − y = sin x?
x: The order is the order of the highest derivative present, d³y/dx³, so it is 3. The 5 is the power of a lower derivative, not the order.

q: Eliminating the arbitrary constant c from y = cx² gives the differential equation:
x: Differentiate: dy/dx = 2cx. From y = cx², c = y/x², so dy/dx = 2y/x, i.e. x·dy/dx = 2y. Check with y = x²: x·2x = 2x² = 2y.

q: The differential equation of the family y = A cos x + B sin x (A, B arbitrary constants) is:
x: y′ = −A sin x + B cos x and y″ = −A cos x − B sin x = −y, so y″ + y = 0. Two constants need a second-order equation, which rules out y′ + y = 0.

q: The general solution of a differential equation of order 3 contains how many arbitrary constants?
x: The general solution of an nth-order differential equation contains n independent arbitrary constants, so order 3 gives 3 constants.

q: The differential equation of the family y = Ae^(2x) + Be^(−2x) is:
x: y′ = 2Ae^(2x) − 2Be^(−2x) and y″ = 4Ae^(2x) + 4Be^(−2x) = 4y, so y″ − 4y = 0. The sign change from e^(−2x) cancels on the second differentiation, so y″ + 4y = 0 is wrong.

q: Which of the following differential equations is of first order and first degree?
x: dy/dx + y = x² has only the first derivative, to power 1. (dy/dx)² + y = 0 is first order but degree 2; the other two are second order.

q: y = e^(kx) is a solution of y″ − 5y′ + 6y = 0 if:
x: Substituting gives (k² − 5k + 6)e^(kx) = 0, so (k − 2)(k − 3) = 0 and k = 2 or 3. Check k = 2: 4 − 10 + 6 = 0. The sign slip gives −2, −3.

q: The differential equation of the family of circles x² + y² = r² (r arbitrary) is:
x: Differentiate x² + y² = r²: 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0, so x + y·dy/dx = 0; r disappears because it is a constant.

q: The order and degree of the differential equation y = x·(dy/dx) + √(1 + (dy/dx)²) are:
x: Write p = dy/dx. Isolate the root and square: (y − xp)² = 1 + p², which expands to a polynomial of degree 2 in p. So the order is 1 and the degree is 2; reading the degree before clearing the root gives 1.

q: The differential equation of the family y = (A + Bx)eˣ (A, B arbitrary constants) is:
x: y′ = (A + B + Bx)eˣ and y″ = (A + 2B + Bx)eˣ. Then y″ − 2y′ + y = (A + 2B + Bx − 2A − 2B − 2Bx + A + Bx)eˣ = 0. Check B = 0, y = eˣ: 1 − 2 + 1 = 0.

q: The general solution of dy/dx = x/y is:
x: Separate: y dy = x dx, so y²/2 = x²/2 + c₁, i.e. y² − x² = c. Moving x² to the wrong side gives y² + x² = c, which belongs to dy/dx = −x/y.

q: The general solution of dy/dx = e^(x − y) is:
x: Write e^(x − y) = eˣ·e^(−y), so e^y dy = e^x dx and e^y = e^x + c. Check: differentiating gives e^y y′ = e^x, i.e. y′ = e^(x − y).

q: The general solution of dy/dx = y/x is:
x: Separate: dy/y = dx/x, so ln|y| = ln|x| + ln|c| and y = cx. xy = c solves dy/dx = −y/x instead.

q: The general solution of (1 + x²) dy = (1 + y²) dx is:
x: Separate: dy/(1 + y²) = dx/(1 + x²), so tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x + c. Integrating 1/(1 + y²) as a logarithm gives the ln and power forms, which are wrong.

q: The solution of dy/dx = 2x with y(0) = 3 is:
x: Integrate: y = x² + c; y(0) = 3 gives c = 3, so y = x² + 3. Check: y′ = 2x and y(0) = 3.

q: If dy/dx = 3y and y(0) = 2, then y at x = ln 2 is:
x: dy/y = 3 dx gives y = Ce^(3x); y(0) = 2 gives C = 2. So y(ln 2) = 2e^(3 ln 2) = 2 × 8 = 16. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 8.

q: The solution of dy/dx = y² with y(0) = 1 is:
x: dy/y² = dx gives −1/y = x + c; y(0) = 1 gives c = −1, so 1/y = 1 − x and y = 1/(1 − x). Check: y′ = 1/(1 − x)² = y². The sign slip in −1/y gives 1/(1 + x).

q: The general solution of sec²x tan y dx + sec²y tan x dy = 0 is:
x: Divide by tan x tan y: (sec²x/tan x) dx + (sec²y/tan y) dy = 0. Integrating gives ln|tan x| + ln|tan y| = ln|c|, so tan x · tan y = c.

q: A curve passes through (0, 1) and its slope at every point (x, y) is 2xy. Its equation is:
x: dy/dx = 2xy gives dy/y = 2x dx, ln y = x² + c; at (0, 1), c = 0, so y = e^(x²). Check: y′ = 2x e^(x²) = 2xy. y = x² + 1 has slope 2x, not 2xy.

q: The general solution of dy/dx = sin x · cos y is:
o: ln|sec y + tan y| = cos x + c
ln|sec y + tan y| = −cos x + c
x: Separate: sec y dy = sin x dx. ∫sec y dy = ln|sec y + tan y| and ∫sin x dx = −cos x, giving the first form. Writing ∫sin x dx = cos x is the sign slip; sin y = −cos x + c comes from multiplying by cos y instead of dividing.

q: If dy/dx = x·e^(−y) and y(0) = 0, the value of y at x = 2 is:
x: e^y dy = x dx gives e^y = x²/2 + c; y(0) = 0 gives c = 1. At x = 2, e^y = 2 + 1 = 3, so y = ln 3. Dropping the ½ gives ln 5; dropping the constant gives ln 2.

q: If dy/dx = y cos x and y(0) = 1, then y(π/2) equals:
x: dy/y = cos x dx gives ln y = sin x + c; y(0) = 1 gives c = 0, so y = e^(sin x). At π/2, sin x = 1, so y = e.

q: If dy/dx = xy + x and y(0) = 0, then y at x = √2 is:
x: Factor: dy/dx = x(y + 1), so dy/(y + 1) = x dx and ln|y + 1| = x²/2 + c. y(0) = 0 gives c = 0, so y = e^(x²/2) − 1, and at x = √2, y = e − 1. Forgetting the −1 gives e.

q: Which differential equation is NOT separable?
x: x + y cannot be written as f(x)·g(y). The others factor: xy = x·y, e^(x + y) = eˣ·e^y, and x²/(y + 1) = x²·1/(y + 1).

q: If (x + 1)·dy/dx = 2y and y(0) = 1, then y(2) equals:
x: dy/y = 2 dx/(x + 1) gives ln y = 2 ln(x + 1) + c; y(0) = 1 gives c = 0, so y = (x + 1)². Then y(2) = 3² = 9. Losing the factor 2 gives y = x + 1 and the answer 3.

q: If y·dy/dx = 2x and y = −2 when x = 1, then y when x = 3 is:
x: y dy = 2x dx gives y²/2 = x² + c; at (1, −2), 2 = 1 + c, c = 1, so y² = 2x² + 2. At x = 3, y² = 20, and y keeps the sign of the starting value, so y = −2√5. Dropping the ½ on y gives y² = x² + 3 and −2√3.

q: A population P grows at a rate proportional to its size: dP/dt = kP, with P = P₀ at t = 0. Then P(t) is:
x: dP/P = k dt gives ln P = kt + c, so P = Ce^(kt); P(0) = P₀ gives C = P₀. P₀e^(−kt) describes decay.

q: A bacteria culture grows at a rate proportional to its size and doubles every 3 hours. If it starts with 500 bacteria, how many are there after 9 hours?
x: Growth proportional to size is exponential: 9 hours is 3 doubling times, so 500 × 2³ = 4000. Adding the same amount each 3 hours (linear growth) gives 2000.

q: A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the amount present and has a half-life of 10 years. What fraction of it remains after 30 years?
x: 30 years is 3 half-lives, so the fraction left is (½)³ = 1/8. Dividing by 3 instead of halving three times gives 1/3.

q: A quantity decays by dN/dt = −kN (k > 0) and halves in time T. Then k equals:
x: N = N₀e^(−kt) and N₀/2 = N₀e^(−kT), so e^(kT) = 2 and k = (ln 2)/T. T/(ln 2) is the inverted form.

q: A population following P = P₀e^(kt) triples in 2 years. How long does it take to become 9 times its starting size?
x: Tripling in 2 years means e^(2k) = 3. Nine times is 3², which needs e^(kt) = (e^(2k))², so t = 4 years. Scaling the time by 9/3 gives the linear answer 6.

q: A boat's speed v (m/s) falls under resistance with dv/dt = −kv. If v = 20 at t = 0 and v = 10 at t = 1 s, then v at t = 3 s is:
x: v = 20e^(−kt) and e^(−k) = ½, so v(3) = 20 × (½)³ = 2.5. Subtracting 10 per second (linear decrease) gives 0.

q: The excess temperature θ of a cooling body over its surroundings satisfies dθ/dt = −kθ. θ falls from 80 °C to 40 °C in 10 minutes. How much longer does it take to fall from 40 °C to 10 °C?
x: θ = θ₀e^(−kt) halves every 10 minutes. From 40 to 10 is two halvings (40 → 20 → 10), so 20 minutes. Counting it as one halving gives 10; treating the fall as linear (4 degrees per minute) gives 7.5.

q: An amount of money A grows continuously at a rate of 5% of the current amount per year. The differential equation for A (t in years) is:
x: The rate of change is 5% of the amount, i.e. 0.05 × A, so dA/dt = 0.05A. Writing 5A forgets to turn the percentage into a decimal.

q: Money grows by dA/dt = 0.05A (t in years). The time for the money to double is:
x: A = A₀e^(0.05t), so 2 = e^(0.05t) and t = (ln 2)/0.05 = 20 ln 2 years. Using 1/0.05 = 20 without the ln 2 gives 20 years.

q: A particle moves along a line so that ds/dt = 2√s, with s = 1 at t = 0. Its displacement s at t = 2 is:
x: ds/√s = 2 dt gives 2√s = 2t + c; at t = 0, √s = 1, so √s = t + 1 and s(2) = 3² = 9. Treating the rate as fixed at its starting value 2 gives s = 1 + 2 × 2 = 5.

q: A town's population P = 1000e^(0.02t) (t in years). What is its rate of growth, in people per year, when P = 1500?
x: dP/dt = 0.02 × 1000e^(0.02t) = 0.02P, so at P = 1500 the rate is 0.02 × 1500 = 30. Using the starting size 1000 gives 20.

q: A radioactive sample decays at a rate proportional to the amount present. After 2 hours only one quarter of it is left. How many MORE hours until only 1/32 of the original is left?
x: One quarter after 2 hours is 2 half-lives, so the half-life is 1 hour. 1/32 = (½)⁵ is reached at t = 5 hours, so 3 more hours. 5 is the total time, not the extra time.
